I.      Introduction

        Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, Clean Air

Task Force, Inc., Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficiency in

Pennsylvania, Earthjustice, Environmental Defense Fund, Montana Environmental

Information Center, Natural Resources Defense Council, Sustainable FERC Project,

Sierra Club, and Southern Environmental Law Center (jointly, the “Public Interest

Organizations”) submit these comments in response to the Commission’s request for

comments on the Department of Energy (“DOE” or “Department”) October 23, 2025

proposal directing FERC to initiate a rulemaking concerning the interconnection of large

loads for final action by the Commission under Section 403 of the Department of Energy

Organization Act1 (“DOE Proposal” or “Proposal”).2

        As noted in the ANOPR, data centers are driving an extraordinary growth in

electricity demand. The North American Electric Reliability Corp (NERC) warned that

the size and speed with which data centers can be connected to the grid present unique

challenges for demand forecasting and system planning.3 The Commission considered

         During the conference, the Commission hosted three panel discussions with a

Monitors to state commissioners. The conference covered many of the issues relevant to

this proceeding including jurisdictional service approaches other than co-location (e.g.,

flexible options), impacts on reliability and resource adequacy, stability of wholesale

electricity market prices, and states’ concerns over affordability and consumer impacts.

Subsequently, on February 20, 2025, the Commission determined that PJM

Interconnection, LLC’s (PJM) tariff provisions for co-location arrangements appeared to

be unjust and unreasonable and initiated a show cause proceeding, which teed up the

retail rate classes. This jurisdictional split in the cost allocation process shifts data center

costs on to other customers.11 Absent sufficient guardrails and information, this new

pollution. While PJM and other RTOs, like the Southwest Power Pool, have initiated

tariff filings or stakeholder processes to integrate large load customers in the near-term,12

DOE’s ANOPR gives the Commission an opportunity to take stock of the record from

interconnecting large loads in the near-term, given the widespread desire for interim

options. Further, a standardized rule itself could help eliminate incentives for seeking

interconnections in multiple regions, helping to create more accurate large load forecasts.

        These comments present preliminary thoughts on the fourteen principles

enunciated in DOE’s Proposal. While DOE’s Proposal articulates numerous important

comments at that time. Our views and comments may evolve as FERC develops its

proposals. Generally, we believe that DOE’s Proposal is correct that the rapid

proliferation of new large loads presents challenges that FERC must address to maintain

a reliable and affordable electric grid. In short, new large loads—principally data

centers—are seeking to connect to the grid much faster than new generation can currently

be interconnected, and the resulting imbalance in demand and supply threatens to

radically increase energy prices and challenge the reliability of electric service. Because

these threats to affordability and reliability are emerging rapidly, FERC should quickly

address how to interconnect large loads under its FPA authority.

       While FERC should act promptly to address immediate affordability and

reliability challenges, FERC must also develop and enhance longer-term transmission

planning and interconnection strategies to ensure that stable planning structures are

sufficient to ensure reliable electric service at just, reasonable, and not unduly

discriminatory rates, and are consistent with longstanding open-access principles. The

Commission’s goal should be to ensure that transmission-planning and interconnection

procedures – for both large loads and generation – are sufficiently rigorous to realistically

assess the growth in demand, anticipate changes in the generation mix, and proactively

plan for the resulting transmission needs. The grid is at an inflection point, and we need

to increase transmission capacity – both within and between regions – to ensure

affordable, reliable electricity while we meet the moment to serve these new loads. New

transmission capacity – regional and interregional, whether gained through grid-

enhancing technologies, advanced conductors, or new transmission build – will bolster

reliability and allow large loads to interconnect more quickly and at least cost.

Connecting load centers to regions with excess supply power can reduce costs and avoid

redundant infrastructure by allowing regions to share their generating resources.14 This

infrastructure can also save customers money - $7.8 billion to $10.6 billion annually

according to a recent study of interregional transmission expansion recommended by

NERC.15 Further, significant capacity gains can be made fairly quickly through the

addition of advanced transmission technologies (ATTs) to the system. ATTs can boost

capacity by an additional 20 to 100 GW of peak demand without building new wires.16

In this rulemaking and other dockets, FERC should consider ways within its authority to

encourage the adoption of these technologies as an additional way to meet growing loads.

        In developing strategies to address the rapid proliferation of new large loads,

whether in the short term or the long term, the Commission should follow the guiding

principle that new large loads should not be permitted to harm affordability or reliability

for existing consumers. Consistent with the Federal Power Act’s (FPA) fundamental cost-

causation principles, new large loads should be responsible for the costs they cause, and it

would be unjust and unreasonable for the costs caused by new large loads to be shifted to

existing consumers who did not cause those costs and who receive no, or trivial, benefits

from the infrastructure developed to serve new large loads. Similarly, new large loads

should not imperil reliability for other consumers; for example, it would not be just and

        Under the DOE Organization Act, FERC has exclusive jurisdiction over the DOE

Proposal.17 After reviewing the comments it receives in response to its notice, FERC

may:

        (1) concur in adoption of the rule or statement as proposed by the Secretary;
        (2) concur in adoption of the rule or statement only with such changes as it may
        recommend; or
        (3) recommend that the rule or statement not be adopted.[18]

        The Secretary’s letter specifically anticipates that “[the Commissioners] and the

Commission's dedicated staff will build upon these principles and work expeditiously to

initiate a rulemaking proceeding and ultimately issue a final rule.” If FERC adopts DOE's

proposal, FERC must provide clear regulations to implement large load interconnection,

consistent with its statutory obligation under the FPA that the rates, terms, and conditions

of service must be just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. We look forward to

seeing how FERC develops these ideas into a more comprehensive proposal.

        Importantly, large load interconnection affects a variety of energy users and

providers, including Tribes. We recommend that FERC consult Tribes pursuant to the

federal government's trust responsibilities.19

II.      Background

         On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy signed an advance notice of

proposed rulemaking entitled Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large

Loads. The Secretary proposed the rule under Section 403 of the DOE Organization Act,

which allows the Department to propose rules, and reasonable timelines for final action

on those rules, for consideration by FERC. The Proposal states that in light of

unprecedented growth of large loads, FERC should standardize interconnection

procedures and agreements for such loads, including those seeking to share a point of

interconnection with new or existing generation facilities (co-located loads).20 DOE

includes a set of fourteen principles it believes should inform FERC’s rulemaking on this

issue.


III.     Comments

         A. FERC has jurisdiction to regulate the interconnection of large loads to the
              transmission system, but must not overstep the boundaries of its jurisdiction

         DOE asserts that the FPA allows the Commission to exercise jurisdiction over the

interconnection of large loads. First, DOE states that large load interconnections are a

"critical component of open access transmission service” akin to generator

interconnections that require minimum terms and conditions to ensure non-discriminatory

practice directly affecting FERC-jurisdictional wholesale electricity rates. Finally, DOE

states that its proposal does not impinge on States' authority over retail electricity sales

because it does not exert jurisdiction over any retail sales to the large load. Principle 1 of

the ANOPR explicitly provides that to avoid even arguably affecting the States'

limited to interconnections directly to transmission facilities, consistent with the

Commission's seven-factor test.22

                  1.     The FPA provides FERC with multiple relevant sources of
                  jurisdiction.

       The FPA grants the Commission several sources of jurisdiction that are relevant to

the regulation of new large load interconnection, including authority over interstate

transmission, the responsibility to ensure just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory wholesale rates by regulating practices that directly affect rates in

wholesale energy markets, and responsibility to ensure electric reliability. As the

Commission works to develop the principles DOE has suggested, it should ground its

proposed rule in these several sources of authority.

       Large loads exist at the intersection of state and federal jurisdiction. DOE’s

ANOPR makes clear that FERC should avoid even arguably affecting the States'

jurisdiction. Thus, as the Commission considers how to proceed on regulating the

interconnection of large loads, it must consider whether its authority presents a sufficient

work seamlessly to interconnect these loads in a manner that prioritizes the protection of

other consumers from unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory rates and

reliability issues.

       Section 206 of the FPA provides FERC with the authority and responsibility to

ensure that the rates and practices within its jurisdiction are just and reasonable.23 As

discussed throughout our comments, the interconnection of large loads can shift costs to

other consumers in an unjust and unreasonable manner. It is incumbent upon FERC to

adopt rules sufficient to ensure that rates subject to FERC’s jurisdiction will be just and

reasonable moving forward. Here, this statutory responsibility means that the

Commission must ensure that the interconnection of new large loads will no longer

impose unjust and unreasonable expenses on other ratepayers.

                             a. FERC’s jurisdiction over interstate transmission

       The FPA authorizes the Commission to regulate “the transmission of electric

energy in interstate commerce.”24 The FPA prohibits “unreasonable rates and undue

discrimination ‘with respect to any transmission or sale subject to the jurisdiction of the

Commission’” and gives FERC the authority and responsibility to remedy the unlawful

rates and discriminatory practices.25 The FPA’s grant of jurisdiction over interstate

transmission provides clear authority for the Commission to regulate interconnections to

the interstate transmission system.26 DOE’s Proposal suggests that the Commission

should limit any rule in this docket to regulating solely connections to the interstate

transmission system, as defined by FERC’s seven-factor test for distinguishing

transmission infrastructure from distribution infrastructure. PIOs agree that regulating

interconnection to the transmission grid, as opposed to interconnection to the distribution

grid, falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction. Accordingly, we support DOE’s

identification of the Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission as one foundation for

this rulemaking.

                             b. FERC’s jurisdiction over practices directly affecting
                                wholesale electricity rates

       In addition to FERC’s jurisdiction over the transmission of electric energy in

interstate commerce, the FPA also authorizes FERC to regulate “the sale of electric

energy at wholesale in interstate commerce,” which includes the authority to regulate

                               c. FERC’s authority under section 215 of the FPA

        FERC also has jurisdiction to regulate the interconnection of large loads under

FPA section 215. Section 215 of the FPA outlines FERC’s reliability jurisdiction, which

could serve as an avenue for FERC to address the reliability concerns associated with the

interconnection of incoming large loads. Section 215 of the FPA gives FERC jurisdiction

over “all users, owners and operators of the bulk-power system,” and mandates that “[a]ll

users, owners and operators of the bulk-power system shall comply with reliability

standards.”34 A large load interconnected to the transmission system would clearly be a

user of the bulk-power system. Section 215(d)(5) also allows FERC to direct the North

               2.     FERC should continue to be mindful not to overstep its
               jurisdiction by regulating matters that the FPA reserves to the states.


       While it is important for FERC to exercise its jurisdiction over some issues

affecting the interconnection of large loads and their imposition of costs on other

consumers—especially to regulate issues like wholesale market practices where states

lack authority—it is also important for FERC to recognize that the states have authority

here as well. As noted in the DOE ANOPR, FERC must take care not to “even arguably

affect[] the [s]tates' jurisdiction over generation facilities, facilities used in local

distribution or only for the transmission of electric energy in intrastate commerce, or

transmissions consumed by the transmitter.”36 While FERC has the authority to regulate

wholesale sales of electricity in interstate commerce and the transmission of electric

energy in interstate commerce, the law “leaves to the States alone the regulation of ‘any

other sale,” maintaining “a zone of exclusive state jurisdiction,”37

        States have an interest in ensuring resource adequacy and protecting consumers

from cost shifts. Many states have adopted policies that can make it easier to connect

new large loads while also addressing the affordability and reliability of electricity to

other customers.38 Some include measures like requiring a new large load to subsidize

energy efficiency efforts in the local area to free up capacity for the large load while

benefiting local residents and businesses or providing rate relief to certain retail

customers. For example, a recently approved settlement requires three large data center

customers to contribute $500,000 annually for five years towards the Indiana Community

Action Association to be used for low-income assistance, weatherization, and other

programs.39 Other policies seek to grant queue priority for large customers who benefit

state economic development priorities or communities, including the recently approved

Evergy Kansas settlement and the proposed changes to ComEd’s GT&C tariff in

Illinois.40 Importantly, many state utility commissions have either already approved or

are in the process of establishing large load tariffs intended to insulate other customers

from inappropriately bearing the costs utilities incur to interconnect large loads. FERC

must ensure that any rules it adopts do not impede these programs.

       The electric system is complex and sits at the confluence of state and federal

jurisdiction, and FERC and the states have had to work cooperatively on many issues. As

the Supreme Court has noted, the FPA incorporates principles of “cooperative

federalism” with respect to the roles of state and federal regulators in energy regulation.45

For example, the Court has acknowledged the interconnectedness of wholesale and retail

ratemaking, holding in Hughes v. Talen Energy Marketing, that “[s]tates, of course, may

regulate within the domain Congress assigned to them even when their laws incidentally

affect areas within FERC’s domain,”46 while holding in FERC v. Electric Power Supply

Association that “a FERC regulation does not run afoul of [the FPA] just because it

affects—even substantially—the quantity or terms of retail sales.”47 The Court further

established that the FPA “makes federal and state powers ‘complementary’ and

‘comprehensive,’ so that ‘there [will] be no “gaps” for private interests to subvert the

public welfare.”48

       Following with the spirit of the cooperative federalism principles outlined in EPSA

and Hughes, we encourage FERC to set minimum standards governing the

interconnection of new large loads—floors, not ceilings—to allow for more rigorous state

regulation and encourage RTO/ISOs and utilities to work closely with state regulators to

address the incoming large load demands.

       As discussed below with respect to Principle 10, FERC should not allow any

single customer to claim either full or partial rights to the generation from an existing

       Still, we support the concept of studying load with generation to minimize the

the grid. Adding one-off processes can add administrative and modeling complexity to

utility processes that may delay the utility’s timely processing of existing queue requests,

reduce transparency, and further erode stakeholder confidence in the interconnection

adopting separate fast-tracks, and must at least implement safeguards to prevent fast-

automatically assume that the generator will serve only that load without assessing its

Third, FERC should establish guidelines that balance two competing risks: the risk of

IV.    Conclusion

       We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the principles outlined in the DOE

ANOPR. The DOE Proposal is a good start at setting principles for how FERC can

regulate the interconnection of large loads, but there are many details to be worked out. In

doing so, FERC must follow the guiding principle that new large loads should not be

permitted to harm affordability or reliability for existing consumers. New large loads

should be responsible for the costs they cause, they should not be allowed to imperil

reliability for other consumers, and FERC cannot allow utilities to unduly preference

large load customers over other types of customers. We look forward to seeing FERC’s

proposal on these matters.
